CHILD ABDUCTION PREVENTION ORDERS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Alex Morgan · Pat Morgan

DECLARATION REGARDING CHILD ABDUCTION PREVENTION INFORMATION
This information sheet concerns a child custody or visitation proceeding involving Alex Morgan, filed or to be filed in Sacramento County County, California, between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It is prepared to explain California Family Code section 3048 -- the statute that governs (1) certain contents every custody or visitation order must contain, and (2) the specific findings a court must consider, and the specific preventive measures a court may order, when the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate a risk that a party will abduct Alex Morgan. This information sheet does not itself assert that any risk of abduction exists in this matter, does not request or oppose any specific preventive measure, and does not make or substitute for any finding a court is required to make under Family Code section 3048 -- only the court, applying section 3048 to the evidence and facts of the case before it, can make that determination.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3048(A): CONTENTS REQUIRED IN EVERY CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
Family Code section 3048(a) is not limited to cases involving a risk of abduction: it states that, notwithstanding any other law, in a proceeding to determine child custody or visitation, every custody or visitation order shall contain (1) the basis for the court's exercise of jurisdiction, (2) the manner in which notice and opportunity to be heard were given, (3) a clear description of the custody and visitation rights of each party, (4) a provision stating that a violation of the order may subject the violating party to civil or criminal penalties, or both, and (5) identification of the country of habitual residence of the child or children. As fetched and verified, subdivision (a)'s five requirements apply generally to every custody or visitation order issued in a California proceeding to determine custody or visitation -- the statutory text does not condition subdivision (a) on any prior finding, or even any suspicion, that a risk of abduction exists. The abduction-risk-specific provisions of the statute -- the court's duty to consider risk factors and preventive measures -- are addressed separately in subdivision (b), covered in other clauses of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding any other law, in a proceeding to determine child custody or visitation with a child, every custody or visitation order shall contain all of the following: (1) The basis for the court’s exercise of jurisdiction. (2) The manner in which notice and opportunity to be heard were given. (3) A clear description of the custody and visitation rights of each party. (4) A provision stating that a violation of the order may subject the party in violation to civil or criminal penalties, or both. (5) Identification of the country of habitual residence of the child or children."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(a), required contents of every custody or visitation order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3048.)
  Known gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivision (a) is one subdivision of a single statutory section, so it is one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Family Code requires a California custody or visitation order to contain -- not a claim about what any other state requires, and not a claim about what any specific court has ordered or will order in any individual case. Correction of a naive assumption: subdivision (a)'s five required order contents are NOT limited to abduction-risk cases -- they apply to every custody or visitation order in a California proceeding to determine custody or visitation, regardless of whether abduction risk is ever raised. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear, mandatory statutory text ("every custody or visitation order shall contain all of the following") rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3048(B)(1): THE COURT'S DUTY TO CONSIDER ABDUCTION RISK FACTORS
Family Code section 3048(b)(1) states that in cases in which the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate a risk of abduction of a child, the court shall, either on its own motion or at the request of a party, determine whether measures are needed to prevent the abduction of the child by one parent. In making that determination, the court is directed to consider the risk of abduction of the child, obstacles to the child's location, recovery, and return if the child is abducted, and potential harm to the child if the child is abducted. Section 3048(b)(1) then enumerates eight specific factors the court shall consider to determine whether a risk of abduction exists: (A) whether a party has previously taken, enticed away, kept, withheld, or concealed a child in violation of another person's right of custody or visitation; (B) whether a party has previously threatened to do any of those things; (C) whether a party lacks strong ties to California; (D) whether a party has strong familial, emotional, or cultural ties to another state or country, including foreign citizenship -- a factor the statute says shall be considered only if evidence exists in support of another listed factor; (E) whether a party has no financial reason to stay in California; (F) whether a party has engaged in planning activities that would facilitate removing the child from the state, with consideration given to whether the party is instead carrying out a safety plan to flee from domestic violence; (G) whether a party has a history of a lack of parental cooperation or child abuse, or there is substantiated evidence a party has perpetrated domestic violence; and (H) whether a party has a criminal record. As fetched and verified, these eight factors are stated directly in section 3048(b)(1) itself -- the statute does not cross-reference the Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act (UCAPA) or any other named uniform act for this risk-factor list.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In cases in which the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate that there is a risk of abduction of a child, the court shall, either on its own motion or at the request of a party, determine whether measures are needed to prevent the abduction of the child by one parent. To make that determination, the court shall consider the risk of abduction of the child, obstacles to location, recovery, and return if the child is abducted, and potential harm to the child if the child is abducted. To determine whether there is a risk of abduction, the court shall consider the following factors:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(1), duty to determine whether abduction-prevention measures are needed, and the factors considered (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3048.)
  "Whether a party has engaged in planning activities that would facilitate the removal of a child from the state, including quitting a job, selling the primary residence, terminating a lease, closing a bank account, liquidating other assets, hiding or destroying documents, applying for a passport, applying to obtain a birth certificate or school or medical records, or purchasing airplane or other travel tickets, with consideration given to whether a party is carrying out a safety plan to flee from domestic violence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(1)(F), planning-activities risk factor, and its domestic-violence safety-plan qualifier (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3048.)

Subdivision (b)(1) is one paragraph of a single statutory section and is treated as one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own risk-factor framework -- not a claim that any other state uses the same factors, and not a claim about whether these factors are, or are not, present in any specific case. Correction of a naive research assumption: the eight risk factors are NOT drawn by cross-reference from the Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act (a model act that a number of other states have enacted) -- as verified, the phrase "Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act" does not appear anywhere in section 3048's text, and California has codified its own, separately worded list of risk factors directly within section 3048(b)(1) rather than adopting UCAPA. Section 3048(b)(1) does cross-reference a different uniform act -- the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act -- but only later, within subdivision (b)(2)(J)'s list of preventive measures, covered in a separate clause of this document; that cross-reference does not supply the risk-factor list itself. No case law is cited in this clause; the risk factors are stated in enumerated statutory text rather than developed through contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3048(B)(2): PREVENTIVE MEASURES THE COURT MAY ORDER
Family Code section 3048(b)(2) states that if the court makes a finding that there is a need for preventative measures after considering the risk factors in section 3048(b)(1), the court shall consider taking one or more of eleven listed categories of measures to prevent the abduction of the child: (A) ordering supervised visitation; (B) requiring a parent to post a bond sufficient to serve as a financial deterrent to abduction, whose proceeds may offset the cost of recovering the child if an abduction occurs; (C) restricting the custodial or noncustodial parent's right to remove the child from the county, the state, or the country; (D) restricting the custodial parent's right to relocate with the child unless advance notice and the noncustodial parent's written agreement, or the court's approval, are obtained first; (E) requiring the surrender of passports and other travel documents; (F) prohibiting a parent from applying for a new or replacement passport for the child; (G) requiring a parent to notify a relevant foreign consulate or embassy of passport restrictions and to provide the court with proof of that notification; (H) requiring registration of a California order in another state, or an order from another country with identical terms, as a prerequisite to the child traveling there for visits; (I) obtaining assurances a traveling parent will return from foreign visits, such as a travel itinerary, copies of round-trip airline tickets, a list of addresses and telephone numbers where the child can be reached, or an open airline ticket for the left-behind parent; (J) including provisions to facilitate use of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act and the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, such as identifying California as the child's home state or the United States as the child's country of habitual residence; and (K) authorizing the assistance of law enforcement. Section 3048(b)(3) further states that if the court imposes any of these conditions, they shall be specifically noted on the minute order of the court proceedings.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3048(B)(2)(J): RELATIONSHIP TO THE UCCJEA AND THE HAGUE CONVENTION
Among the preventive measures listed in Family Code section 3048(b)(2), subdivision (J) authorizes the court to consider including provisions in the custody order to facilitate use of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Part 3, commencing with section 3400) and the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (implemented pursuant to 42 U.S.C. section 11601 et seq.). As fetched and verified, examples the statute itself gives include identifying California as the child's home state or otherwise defining the basis for the California court's exercise of jurisdiction under the UCCJEA, identifying the United States as the child's country of habitual residence under the Hague Convention, defining custody rights under the Hague Convention, and obtaining the parents' express agreement that the United States is the child's country of habitual residence or that California or the United States is the most appropriate forum for custody and visitation orders. This measure connects section 3048's abduction-prevention framework to the UCCJEA's separate jurisdictional framework (Family Code sections 3400-3465, addressed in this corpus's separate Child Custody Jurisdiction (UCCJEA) Information Sheet) and to the Hague Convention's separate international framework -- section 3048 does not itself restate the UCCJEA's jurisdictional rules or the Hague Convention's return procedures; it authorizes a California custody order to include provisions that make later use of those other frameworks more effective.

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Family Code authorizes a court to include in a custody order -- not a claim about the current substantive content of the UCCJEA's jurisdictional rules or the Hague Convention's return procedures, neither of which was independently re-verified in this clause (the UCCJEA's home-state and jurisdictional provisions are separately verified in this corpus's Child Custody Jurisdiction (UCCJEA) Information Sheet). This clause exists to make an accurate distinction, not to duplicate that other document: section 3048(b)(2)(J) is a preventive measure a court may include in a custody order in an abduction-risk case, while the UCCJEA document addresses which state's courts have jurisdiction to hear a custody case in the first place -- related but legally distinct questions. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by direct statutory cross-reference rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3048(B)(4): REQUIRED NOTICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY'S CHILD ABDUCTION UNIT
Family Code section 3048(b)(4) states that if the court determines there is a risk of abduction sufficient to warrant applying one or more of the prevention measures the statute authorizes, the court shall inform the parties of the telephone number and address of the Child Abduction Unit in the office of the district attorney in the county where the custody or visitation order is being entered. Section 3048(c) separately directs the Judicial Council to make the changes to its child custody order forms necessary to implement subdivision (b). Section 3048(d) states that section 3048 does not affect the applicability of Penal Code section 278.7 -- meaning, as fetched and verified, that section 3048's civil custody-order provisions and Penal Code section 278.7 (a distinct statute addressing custodial interference in violation of a court order) each continue to apply on their own terms; section 3048 does not state that it modifies, limits, or replaces Penal Code section 278.7.
